claims.case_section: Phase I: Irish *fáinne* and the Anglo-Irish *Fawney* Chain (1768–1867)
claims.short_label: 1781–1889 British thieves'-cant chronology and transatlantic American transmission of fawney ('gilt-brass confidence ring')
claims.statement: Primary scans track British cant fawney ('gilt-brass ring used in confidence drops and street wager-bouncing') from Parker (1781), Grose (1788/1796), Potter ([1795]), Vaux (1812), 1827 Old Bailey testimony, and Mayhew/Ducange/Hotten (1851–1859) into American print across 1843–1889 (Spirit of the Times 1843, Matsell 1859, Clipper 1860, Philadelphia Telegraph 1867, Barrère & Leland 1889).
claims.rationale: Crossbarred-F verification in 1781, live 1827 Old Bailey speech, and Matsell's active 1859 New York emendation of Ducange's 'sawney' typo establish continuous Anglo-American underworld usage.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Continuous 1781–1889 British and Eastern Seaboard American print attestation of cant fawney / fauny for gilt-brass rings.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: North American vowel closing to /foʊni/ or <ph-> respelling (evaluated in CLM-2200-006).
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Extent of spoken street circulation between 1868 and 1888 (bounded in CLM-2200-007).

limitations: Matsell 1859 (313) vs. Worthington c. 1877 (314) and Hotten 1859 (201/312) are deduplicated via CLM-2200-009.

claims.case_section: Phase I: Irish *fáinne* and the Anglo-Irish *Fawney* Chain (1768–1867)

evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Direct pre-1781 bilingual London magistrate depositions.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Recovering 1740–1780 St Giles court examinations preserving code-switching between Irish fáinne and cant fawney.

limitations: Pre-1781 oral borrowing rests on comparative phonological and semantic alignment.
resolution_criteria: Inspect 1740–1780 Middlesex/Bow Street examinations of St Giles Irish defendants for transitional spellings.

evidence.reason: O'Brien 1768 Irish áinne / fáinne ('ring').
O'Reilly 1817 ('vulg. fáinne') and Dinneen 1904 ('fáinne an phósta').
Meyer & Sampson 1890–1891 proving Shelta encrypted fáinne as gránya.
